children.text: I'm trying to organize about 400k photos. What kind of questions are you asking it and what are you doing with that info? Applying tags/labels? Sorting into albums?

Image input is a primary reason I've never moved off my "home rolled" version of Jev (that Claude wrote for me over a year ago) for my file organizer/indexer. Takes images resizes them to 1k, then asks a handful of questions about the image for tagging purposes. It is able to process around 3 images a second based on Qwen 3 VL, but distilled and optimized for 1k images and up to 2048 token inputs (after the system prompt, then the questions are asked one after each other reusing the cache). Documents that are longer than that end up going through a summarizer that runs on my other GPU (Qwen 3.6, I think). And all of that gets fed into a vector search engine, for easy lookup later.

I'm not even sure what all is going on inside it anymore, because I just add new features when they popup, and tell Claude to do it, and it let's me know when it is done, and every new "input feature" can run against the entire catalogue of files.

Its bit more expensive than other other Decision Models in the same lane.

However, it can accept Audio and Video as input as well and for those specific cases it can be extremely useful.

children.author: coderenegade
children.text: In my experience, calibration is only ever in expectation, even for a classic classifier. Any given prediction is often still over- or under-confident.

The thing I had to wrap my head around is: For a "classic" classifier, the classes are fixed and the data distribution is p(x,y). The calibration is checked over this single distribution. Jev makes the tasks part of the input, so the data distribution is p(task,x,y) and calibration is averaged over that joint distribution. What follows is that while for classic classifiers, calibration brakes down if your x was out-of-distribution, it can now also break if your task is out of distribution. The big question now is: Can subtle differences in phrasing your task already lead to this? And the only way to verify calibration is having ground truth data to validate on.
Also: Calibration over p(task, x, y) means calibrated on average across tasks. Even an in-distribution task can be over- or underconfident while the average looks fine.

For a single prediction, sure. But the model doesn't make a single prediction and then stop existing. It makes an unbounded number of future predictions and under that assumption it is reasonable to expect the model to behave optimally under Bayes rule - which has a unique global minimizer at E[(Y-F(X))^2].

So counter to your claim that "It doesn't trivially imply that the model would learn sensible distributions under uncertainty" I think you need to consider what it means to optimally update a posterior under the global minimizer of the true conditional distribution.

Zero-shot encoders even pre-date LLMs. People who worked in NLP in the transformers "BERT-era" may be familiar with natural language inference (NLI).

Decision models are really not much different than that, but (usually) scaled up to bigger causal models.

We were doing zero and few-shot classification with LLMs since before they could reliably complete whole sentences. It’s an easier task than generating coherent text. The model needed to be tuned for classification (not generation) and for the domain, but it would often succeed at new classification tasks with a simple description.

I guess given the huge advances in LLM since then, these models probably achieve much better accuracy on a wide range of domains with lower effort compared to what we were doing, which makes it compelling as a product. children.author: nlpnerd
children.text:
Basically there is a whole host of tarpit usage of LLMs in application backends today. This is simply another case of LLMs enabling people to build what they cannot productionize or maintain.

Today developers without any AI/ML skillset can prototype a fancy new feature with LLMs, what used to require collecting and curating data to train a pipeline of ML models then serving them in production.

The problem comes when it's time to take the new feature into production. That $20 cost with prototype/beta workload is now $30k per month in LLM costs, and those hallucinations that never happened on their 200 test samples is happening 600 times per day.

They are then stuck, because they lack the knowledge and budget to build and run the production ML pipeline properly, the infra stack necessary to handle production workload. Management also doesn't understand why they have to invest in rebuilding something that "seems to work" with "outdated methods".

These system one or decision models are a step up from LLMs when it comes to this usage. Problem is that they are still difficult to work with (limited in expression power) for many application logic. Despite the initial popularity, I hear about a lot of frictions refactoring LLM based backend with them, and multiple cases of production rollbacks to LLMs already.

I think system one models is a sensible paradigm, but there is a lot more work needed above the model layer to make this work.

Task classification - given a set of classes, return the most likely class for each task

Guardrails - check the text against a set of guardrail checks (questions)

Search - Given a search criteria, I first have an LLM generate a query that would go to the decision model. This query is a rubric that scores each document. children.author: Topfi
children.text:
Audio, Video and File input? That is very appealing and I can imagine a few very unique ways to leverage this if it works well across all modalities.

For what it's worth, ran my quick and dirty evals with it and got in many usage scenarios a 4x lower brier over Jev (2x - 6x depending on task), which is an immense improvement and the first time a model so significantly has outperformed Jev in my experience. p50 was also over 100ms lower though all this cost twice as much across the entire eval end-to-end.

Dare I say, this is a very impressive release by the Gemini team. While testing GPT-6 Luna lead to an honestly very pleasant interaction with OpenAI staff on here, it did perform very uncompetitively so seeing a great first effort in basic text classification performance with broad multimodality, that is great to see. Course, wouldn't be surprised if Google had such a more broadly trained classifier for years as part of internal usage for platform features which they just now commercialised, but hey, I'll take it.
